title: IAM principals: user, group, role and federated identity

videos.script: An AWS account has more than one kind of identity, and they are not interchangeable. {{root}} The first is the root user, made from the e-mail address that opened the account. It can do anything, and that is exactly why nobody works as root. {{users}} Next come IAM users. A user has a password, an access key, or both. Both last until somebody deletes them. {{groups}} Groups gather users, so that permissions follow a team rather than a person. But a group never signs a request. It is a list, not an identity. {{roles}} A role is the opposite. It has permissions and no credentials at all. A principal assumes it, and gets a session that expires on its own, by default after an hour. {{federation}} Federation goes one step further. Somebody else signs the identity in, GitHub, for the shop's deployments. AWS trusts that signature and hands out a role session. No key is stored anywhere. {{arns}} In this lesson you create each of them in moto, and read the names AWS gives them. The ARN, the unique id, and the four letters at the front of every key. {{end}}
